world_behind.title: A farewell in Moses' form
world_behind.text: Rehearsal of mercies, covenant terms, blessings and cursings, succession: Lehi's last sermon runs Deuteronomy's outline, down to Moses' own idiom ("the statutes and the judgments" (v. 16)). The record has cast Lehi as the new exodus's Moses since the wilderness; here he dies like him, preaching the covenant at the border of the inheritance.

world_behind.title: Deathbed formulas of kings
world_behind.text: "I go the way of all the earth" (v. 14) is the sentence Joshua and David each spoke at the end (Josh. 23:14; 1 Kgs. 2:2), and David followed it, as Lehi does, with the charge to act like men. The old leaders' farewell genre is audible under the trembling parent's voice.

cites.quote: I go the way of all the earth

spans.text: I go the way of all the earth

world_behind.title: The isolation clause
world_behind.text: "This land should be kept as yet from the knowledge of other nations" (v. 8): the covenant includes geography as strategy. An unknown land cannot be overrun, and the record will treat the age of discovery (1 Ne. 13) as this clause expiring on schedule rather than failing.

cites.quote: This land should be kept as yet from the knowledge of other nations

spans.text: This land should be kept as yet from the knowledge of other nations

world_behind.title: Land grants ran on conditions
world_behind.text: Ancient covenant treaties deeded territory the way verse 7 does: tenure held of a sovereign, kept by loyalty, forfeited by breach. Lehi's hearers knew inheritance law that worked exactly so; what is new is the sovereign ("consecrated unto him") and the scale, a hemisphere held on the terms of a vassal's fidelity.

world_behind.title: The accusations had a history
world_behind.text: Every charge Lehi answers in verses 24–27 was filed years earlier: ruler-ambition at the Red Sea (1 Ne. 16:37–38), hard words on the ship (17:48 and 18:10). A dying father speaking to grown men rehearses the family's whole litigation, and the record preserves his brief because the case reopens the moment he is buried (2 Ne. 5:3).

world_behind.title: Zoram, the first grafted branch
world_behind.text: Laban's servant, bound once by an oath (1 Ne. 4:35), leaves the chapter a covenant heir: "because thou hast been faithful thy seed shall be blessed with his seed" (v. 31). The family's promises prove extendable beyond blood one chapter before Jacob's olive-tree doctrine says they must be.

cites.quote: because thou hast been faithful thy seed shall be blessed with his seed

spans.text: because thou hast been faithful thy seed shall be blessed with his seed

words.text: Lehi "rehearsed unto them, how great things the Lord had done for them" (v. 1): re-hearing as the first act of the farewell. The mercies are not new information to the sons who lived them; they are told again because covenant memory decays without recital, and the sermon's warnings will lean on the history just re-laid.

cites.quote: rehearsed unto them, how great things the Lord had done for them

spans.text: rehearsed unto them, how great things the Lord had done for them

words.text: The land is "consecrated unto him whom he shall bring" (v. 7): set apart, made sacred to a purpose. The word turns real estate into stewardship, and it brackets the sermon (v. 32 repeats it over Zoram's seed): what the Lord consecrates, conduct keeps or forfeits.

cites.quote: consecrated unto him whom he shall bring

spans.text: consecrated unto him whom he shall bring

words.text: Nobody decides to dwindle. Treated at 1 Nephi 4:13. The verb is for gradual loss, thinning away without a moment of decision, and it is this record's standing word for how belief ends: "they shall dwindle in unbelief" (v. 10). What makes the line heavy is the inventory Lehi wraps around it, knowledge of the creation, power to do all things by faith, "all the commandments from the beginning" (v. 10). An estate that size can still be mislaid slowly. No one in the King James Bible ever dwindles; in this volume the word turns up wherever a people is losing its faith by degrees.

cites.quote: all the commandments from the beginning

spans.text: all the commandments from the beginning

words.text: One who journeys, and here the word for whoever might come back from the grave. It appears once in this record and never in the King James Bible. Lehi points at the ground his own limbs are going into, "from whence no traveler can return" (v. 14). This family had spent eight years as travelers, through a wilderness and across an ocean; the one trip he names as having no return leg is the one he is about to take.

cites.quote: from whence no traveler can return

spans.text: from whence no traveler can return

words.text: Its first appearance in the record: "this hath been the anxiety of my soul from the beginning" (v. 16). The word will become the standing term for what prophets and parents carry (Jacob and Alma inherit it for their own sermons): concern for souls, chronic, clarifying, and openly confessed.

spans.text: this hath been the anxiety of my soul from the beginning

words.text: The accusation quoted and reforged: "his sharpness was the sharpness of the power of the word of God" (v. 26). What they heard as a brother's temper was, on the father's testimony, the instrument's edge. The record keeps the word for later hard sermons; whether sharpness wounds or heals depends on whose power it carries.

cites.quote: his sharpness was the sharpness of the power of the word of God

spans.text: his sharpness was the sharpness of the power of the word of God

phrases.text: Coined here, over the new land, with its condition in the same breath: liberty for those who serve the God who consecrated it. The phrase becomes the record's political north star (2 Ne. 10:11; Mosiah 29:32; Alma 46:17), and every later loss of freedom is diagnosed on this verse's terms: captivity enters only "because of iniquity" (v. 7).

Lehi's figure makes rebellion unconsciousness: "awake from a deep sleep, yea, even from the sleep of hell" (v. 13), with chains that bind sleepers who never felt them fastened. The diagnosis is merciful: the sleepers are unconscious, and the remedy is reveille, sounded four times across the sermon.

cites.quote: awake from a deep sleep, yea, even from the sleep of hell

spans.text: awake from a deep sleep, yea, even from the sleep of hell

phrases.term: Encircled about eternally in the arms of his love
phrases.text: The sermon's testimony sentence, and its geometry: against the "chains" (v. 13) that bind downward stands another enclosure, arms, eternal, chosen. Lehi does not ask his sons for anything he is not already inside of; the redeemed father describes the embrace from within it.

phrases.term: Inasmuch as ye shall keep my commandments
phrases.text: The covenant formula of the valley (1 Ne. 2:20), quoted now as the sermon's legal center: "ye shall prosper in the land" (v. 20), with the counter-clause spoken aloud this time: "cut off from my presence" (v. 20). First given to Nephi alone, it is here published to the whole family; the record will requote it for a thousand years.

cites.quote: ye shall prosper in the land

spans.text: ye shall prosper in the land

phrases.term: Arise from the dust, my sons, and be men
phrases.text: David's deathbed charge to Solomon ran the same way: I go the way of all the earth; be thou strong, show thyself a man. Lehi's version adds the dust, defeat, death, and sleep in one noun, and aims the manhood at unity: "determined in one mind and in one heart, united in all things" (v. 21).

cites.quote: determined in one mind and in one heart, united in all things

phrases.term: It was not he, but it was the Spirit
phrases.text: The defense's closing argument: the compulsion his brothers resented ( "his commanding you that ye must obey" (v. 27)) had a source outside the brother: "which opened his mouth to utterance that he could not shut it" (v. 27). The sentence gives the record its test for hard words: ask whose mouth it came out of.

verses.label: v. 7–9
verses.title: A deathbed sermon whose commonest word is real estate
verses.text: Land is used twenty-six times here, which places this chapter fourth in all of scripture for the word, behind Genesis 47 and two Alma chapters that are surveys. Verse 7 then fits the whole covenant and its reversal into one sentence: served, it is liberty and no captivity; if captivity comes it will be for iniquity; iniquity curses the land and righteousness blesses it. Verse 8 gives the reason for keeping the place secret, and the reason is crowding rather than mystery: other nations "would overrun the land, that there would be no place for an inheritance."

verses.label: v. 17–18
verses.title: The fear is itemized before the plea is made
verses.text: What Lehi says he has feared is set out in order: wrath, being cut off and destroyed forever, a cursing across many generations, visitation by sword and by famine, hatred, and captivity to the devil's will. Six outcomes across two verses. He does not ask for anything until verse 19, and by then the reader knows exactly what he is asking them to avoid.

verses.label: v. 20
verses.title: The promise is quoted with both halves attached
verses.text: Prosper in the land for keeping the commandments, cut off from the presence for not. Lehi does not paraphrase it or soften the second clause, and he attributes it rather than asserting it: "he hath said that." Alma will hand his own son the same sentence at Alma 36, and give the positive half first and the negative half twenty-nine verses later.

verses.label: v. 21–23
verses.title: One phrase, three times, and scripture has one other
verses.text: "Arise from the dust" falls at verses 14, 21 and 23; scripture uses it four times in all. Each carries a different load: at 14 it answers a grave being dug, at 21 it is joined to becoming men and being of one mind, at 23 it follows armor, chains and obscurity. The record keeps the wording identical and lets it gather three arguments.

verses.label: v. 24
verses.title: The defence of Nephi concedes what was done to him
verses.text: Lehi argues his son's case on record: his views have been glorious, he has kept the commandments, he has been an instrument, and without him "we must have perished with hunger in the wilderness." Then the admission, in the same verse, of what the brothers did: "ye sought to take away his life; yea, and he hath suffered much sorrow because of you." The record lets one verse carry the commendation and the accusation together, and gives the last clause to the injury.

chapter.title: Deuteronomy, performed once more
chapter.text: The dying lawgiver rehearses the exodus, publishes the covenant's conditions, sets blessing against cursing, and hands succession to the faithful younger man. The record opens its second book by staging the Pentateuch's close, and it expects readers to hear the rhyme.

chapter.title: The constitutional chapter
chapter.text: Verse 7 legislates for the whole record: liberty conditioned on service, captivity entering only by iniquity, the land cursed or blessed by its people's conduct. Every pride cycle, war, and deliverance for the next thousand years is this covenant executing its terms.

chapter.title: Two enclosures
chapter.text: The sermon draws captivity and salvation with the same shape: chains that bind sleepers down, arms that encircle eternally. Nobody in Lehi's account of the soul stands outside every circle; the only question the sermon leaves its hearers is which enclosure they will wake inside.

chapter.title: Sin as sleep
chapter.text: The chapter's word for the brothers' state is slumber, four times summoned awake. The figure is strategic mercy: a sleeper can be roused without being conquered, and a father can shout reveille where a judge could only sentence.

chapter.title: How prophets get dismissed
chapter.text: Three charges are quoted and answered in two verses. Verse 25: "ye have accused him that he sought power and authority over you." Verse 26: "Ye say that he hath used sharpness; ye say that he hath been angry with you." Each answer relocates the cause rather than denying the conduct: "his sharpness was the sharpness of the power of the word of God," and, at verse 27, "it was not he, but it was the Spirit of the Lord which was in him, which opened his mouth to utterance that he could not shut it." The same three accusations are made in the brothers' own words at 1 Nephi 16:37 and 1 Nephi 18:10.

chapter.title: The floating birthright
chapter.text: The first blessing attaches to hearkening, not to Laman's seniority; it can rest on the accusers or transfer to the accused. The doctrine quietly settles the succession crisis before Lehi dies, and 2 Nephi 5 will show the covenant executing exactly as spoken.

chapter.title: The covenant's first adoption
chapter.text: Zoram's sealing shows the promises are entered by faithfulness, not lineage, one chapter before this book argues it doctrinally. What the olive tree will teach in figure, the family has already done in fact.

applications.title: Rehearse the deliverances
applications.text: Before the next hard family conversation, do what Lehi did first: recite, out loud, the specific rescues your household has already received. Warnings land differently on ground prepared by remembered mercy.

applications.title: Read your liberty as maintained
applications.text: List the freedoms you treat as permanent fixtures, civic and personal, and ask what conduct actually maintains each one. In the covenant's math, liberty is a thing you maintain.

applications.title: Find the comfortable chain
applications.text: The chains of the sermon bind sleepers who do not feel them. Name the one habit that would alarm you if you saw it on someone you love, and treat your own comfort with it as the anesthesia the sermon says it is.

applications.title: Testify inside the warning
applications.text: When anxiety for someone makes you speak, follow Lehi's order: put what God has done for you in the same breath as what you fear for them. A warning without the encircling arms is only a forecast.

applications.title: Defend the plain speaker
applications.text: When someone's accurate words are being repriced as anger or ambition, say in public what Lehi said: the sharpness is the truth's, not the speaker's. The accused prophet in the room is usually defended too late.

applications.title: Bless beyond blood
applications.text: Find your Zoram: the person faithful to your family who is not family, and formalize the bond. Say the blessing, include their people in your people's plans; covenants grow by adoption.

questions.text: Which of my family's deliverances have my children never heard me rehearse?
What iniquity, mine or ours, is currently the likeliest door for captivity into the freedoms I most prize?
What would waking up actually change in my week: which chain would come off first?
Can I describe being encircled in God's love from inside the experience, as Lehi does, or only report about it?
Whose sharpness have I been calling anger, and what would change if I asked whose power was in it?
Where does my inheritance currently rest on my hearkening, and how is my hearing?
